title: How an architecture studio should write an about page
metaTitle: How an architecture studio writes an about page
excerpt: An architecture about page should name who does the work and why that matters to this client. Keep an origin story only when it changes the decision to start a project.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky, a distant skyline that cannot stand in for the people who run a practice.
caption: A skyline with no one in it. The about page still has to name a person. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on an architecture about page?
faqs.answer: The people who will do the work, the roles a client will actually meet, and the kind of site that fits the office. A short note on how you practice is enough if it changes the decision to start a project conversation. Awards, a long timeline, and a city skyline do not substitute for a name.

faqs.question: Should we tell the studio origin story?
faqs.answer: Tell it only when a detail changes the client's decision. A weekly site visit by the person who drew the scheme can matter. The year two founders met at school usually does not. If the story does not help someone with a real site choose, leave it off this page.

faqs.question: How many people should we name?
faqs.answer: Name the people a client will email, meet, or see on site. A large group portrait with no roles is harder to use than four short entries. If the office is one person, say so. Pretending a larger team is a different kind of untruth.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
An architecture studio about page is proof that specific people stand behind the work. Name who does the work, and why a client judging taste before competence should care. Skip the origin myth unless it changes their decision to start a project conversation.

The projects already argued for taste. This page argues for custody. Who draws. Who goes to site. Who answers when the builder asks a question the render never raised. A skyline, a manifesto, and a founding year do not answer that.

## People, not a poster

Open on a person the client might meet. A photograph in the office or on a site, with their name and their role in a sentence. "Ada Khan leads the house projects and attends the weekly site meeting" is an about page doing its job. "We are passionate about place" is a poster.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) puts weight on who created the work. Visitors should be able to tell who is behind a page, and bylines should lead somewhere that explains the person. An architecture office is not a newspaper, but the same test applies. If the only name on the site is the practice name, a careful client has to guess who will hold their job.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for a descriptive, concise title and a clear main heading. "About" is a habit. "Who works on your house" is a summary. Use the plainer heading if it matches the truth. Keep the browser title specific enough that it cannot be confused with the homepage.

Do not open on an anonymous photograph of towers. A distant skyline says the city exists. It does not say your office exists. If you need a picture before the portraits, use a site you built, with the people who ran it, or the desk where the drawings are made. The reader is trying to hire a practice, not to admire a downtown.

## Who does the work

List roles in the order a client experiences them. The person who takes the first conversation. The person who leads design. The person who will be on site. If one human does all three, say that once. It is often a relief. Small offices lose work when the website implies a crowd and the meeting reveals a pair.

For each person, three lines are enough:

- Name and role.
- The kind of project they actually run.
- The part of the job they stay with: design, documentation, construction, or all of it.

Skip hobbies unless they change the work. A principal who also teaches construction detailing has a fact the client can use. A principal who loves skiing does not, on this page. You can be a full human in person. The page is a decision tool.

If people are registered, licensed, or chartered, say the fact without turning it into a crest. Clients hiring for a house often want to know a qualified architect is responsible. Say who signs. Do not invent a wall of affiliations to look larger.

Keep portraits current. A team page with someone who left two years ago is a trust problem the moment a client notices. The page should be editable by the office, not trapped in a designed image. On a Hanabi build, the marketing site is something the client can keep updating. Names are the field that goes stale first.

Group portraits can sit beside the list. They cannot replace it. A reader cannot hover a face in a printed sense and learn who leads alterations. Give each person a name that is text, not a label burned into a photograph.

## Why this client should care

Taste got them here. The about page has to connect these people to this client's problem. That means naming the kind of work, the scale, and the way you stay involved. "We care about craft" is available to every office. "The person who draws the stair is the person who reviews it on site" is a reason.

Write two or three sentences that only your office could sign. The region you know well enough to anticipate the planning issues. The building type you have repeated until the details are calm. The decision to take fewer jobs so construction visits actually happen. If a sentence still works when you swap in a competitor's name, cut it.

Point at the work. "These are the house alterations Ada has led" with three links is stronger than a paragraph of adjectives. The about page can be short because the proof pages are long. Its job is to attach names to that proof.

Say the limit. If you do not take work outside a city, or you do not take developer rollouts, the about page can repeat the boundary in human form. "We are a house practice. We are the wrong office for a shopping centre." The right client feels looked after. The wrong client leaves before the meeting. Both are good outcomes.

Avoid a ranking of values with no behavior attached. Quality, care, and collaboration are the start of a sentence. Finish the sentence with the behavior: how many projects a lead holds, who attends the site meeting, how drawing sets are checked. Behavior is what a skeptical client can test later.

## When an origin story earns its place

Most origin stories do not change the decision. Two people met at school. A practice was founded in a good year. The city was a character. None of that tells a client whether you can handle their party wall.

Keep a detail when it predicts the work. You started by altering your own terrace, and alterations are still the core of the office. You left a large firm because you wanted to stay on site through construction, and that is still the offer. The story is allowed because it is evidence of the boundary, not because it is charming.

Put that detail after the names and the roles. Readers who need the myth can have it. Readers who need to know who to email should not have to survive it first. A page that begins in 2009 and mentions the client in paragraph six has the order backwards.

If the only interesting thing about the founding is the taste of the early work, link to those projects. Let the buildings carry the history. The about page does not need to novelize it.

Read the story to someone who might hire you and ask what they would do differently because of it. If the answer is nothing, the story is for you. Keep it for a talk. Take it off the page that is supposed to start a project conversation.

## What to leave off

Awards can be a short list if they are true and recent, placed after the people. They are not the opening. A client judging taste has already seen the buildings. A medal does not explain who will attend the planning meeting.

Press logos, a map of every city you have visited, and a counter of years in practice are the same class of object. They perform scale. They do not name a person. Use one of them only if a specific client needs that reassurance, and put it low on the page.

Do not publish a philosophy essay that restates the projects in abstract nouns. Light, material, and dwelling can be discussed on a proof page, tied to a wall and a budget. On the about page they often become a way to avoid saying who does the work.

Skip the stock skyline, the drone shot of a city you did not build, and the handshake photograph from a rental library. If you do not have a portrait yet, commission a plain one. A true, slightly ordinary photograph of the people is more useful than a cinematic image of a downtown that is not yours.

The page can end on the same action as the rest of the site. Start a project conversation. One line on what to send. The about page is not a second contact form with new fields. It is the reason they trust the form you already have.

## A page you can keep true

Names change. Roles change. The page has to be editable on a Tuesday without a designer. Treat the entries as content: name, role, paragraph, portrait. A custom layout is welcome. A flattened poster is how the page starts lying.

Hanabi's services include this kind of marketing site: a clear structure, and a build the office can own. If the about page is the piece that keeps drifting into a manifesto, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) and bring the current text. The work is usually a cut, then a plainer heading, then portraits that match the roles. The studio designs and builds. It does not invent a founding myth for you.

Keep the voice identical to the project captions. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. If the projects say "party wall" and the about page says "urban poetry," you have two practices. Pick the one the client met in the work.

Check the page on a phone. The first screen should show a person and a role, not a cropped forehead and a slogan. The path to start a project should still be reachable. An about page that only works as a desktop spread has forgotten the client who is comparing offices on the way home.

## The proof those people can point to

Names without projects slide back into claim. Once the reader knows who leads the work, they will want one job told properly: the constraint, the decision, and the built result. That is a proof page, not another paragraph of biography.

Read [proof pages for an architecture studio](/blog/proof-pages-for-an-architecture-studio) next. The about page attaches a person to the practice. The proof page shows the judgment that person is asking to be hired for.
